interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is that two amounts in proportion make a straight line through (0, 0), so doubling the reading along doubles the reading up, while a line that misses (0, 0), or bends, is not in proportion, and that with voltage up the side a steeper V-I line means more ohms, when you draw a resistor's V-I graph from V = IR, test lines for proportion, compare resistors' lines, swap the axes and judge measured readings.
interactive.title: Straight lines through zero
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens. Each shows a graph whose axes are named with their units: resistors' voltage against current, a call-out bill against hours, a cable drum's weight against its cable, a heater's power against its current and a tank's level against time. Lines and curves are drawn from their rules or from example readings, and a reading cursor runs up from the bottom axis to the line and across to the side. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it.
interactive.ignores: All the amounts are example values, chosen so the numbers come out simply: the resistors' ohms, the call-out's £40 and £30 an hour, the drum's 20 kg and 0.5 kg a metre, the 5 Ω heater, the part's curve, the tank's level and the measured readings. The resistors are taken to keep the same resistance at every current, and the part's bent V-I curve is drawn from example numbers, not from a real component. Steepness is compared by eye only; working it out as a number comes in a later course.

numbers.label: A 5 Ω resistor by V = IR: 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 V at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 A, every point on one straight line through (0, 0), in step 1
A resistor reading 6 V at 2 A on a straight line through (0, 0): at 4 A, 2 × 6 = 12 V, the point (4, 12), not (4, 8) or (4, 6), in step 2
A £40 call-out plus £30 an hour: 40 + 2 × 30 = £100 for 2 h and 40 + 4 × 30 = £160 for 4 h, not 2 × 100 = £200, in step 3
A drum of 20 kg empty plus 0.5 kg a metre of cable: 20 kg at 0 m, 20 + 0.5 × 60 = 50 kg at 60 m, so it misses (0, 0), in step 4
A 5 Ω heater by P = I²R: 2² × 5 = 20 W at 2 A and 4² × 5 = 80 W at 4 A, four times as much, in step 5
An example part's V-I curve through (0, 0), (2, 5), (4, 15) and (6, 30): 15 V at 4 A, not 2 × 5 = 10 V or 4 × 5 = 20 V, in step 6
5 Ω and 10 Ω resistors at 2 A: 2 × 5 = 10 V and 2 × 10 = 20 V, in step 7
Lines for 4 Ω, 8 Ω and 3 Ω resistors (A, B and C): at 3 A they take 12 V, 24 V and 9 V, so line B is the steepest, in step 8
With current up the side, the 5 Ω line runs from (0, 0) to (30, 6) and the 10 Ω line to (30, 3), so the 5 Ω line is the steeper, in step 9
A 3 Ω resistor at 2 A takes 2 × 3 = 6 V; with current up the side and voltage along, its point is (6, 2), not (2, 6) or (5, 2), in step 10
A tank at 20 cm at 0 min, filling 5 cm a minute, has 20 + 5 × 6 = 50 cm at 6 min; on a side from 20 cm it starts in the corner, in step 11
Example readings 0, 6, 8.5, 16.5, 17.5 and 26.5 V at 0 to 5 A; their best-fit line runs from (0, 0) to (5, 25), the 5 Ω line, in step 12

explain.text:
Two amounts are in direct proportion when doubling one doubles the other and 0 goes with 0, as in Proportional reasoning. On a graph, that is a straight line through (0, 0). A resistor's voltage and current work this way. By V = IR, a 5 Ω resistor takes 5 V at 1 A, 10 V at 2 A and 20 V at 4 A, and 0 V at 0 A, so its points lie on one straight line through (0, 0). BBC Bitesize says that when the V-I graph is a straight line that passes through the origin, the current and voltage are proportional.[^1] So along such a line, doubling the current doubles the voltage. A resistor reading 6 V at 2 A reads 12 V at 4 A, not 8 V.

Both parts of the test matter. A £40 call-out plus £30 an hour makes a straight line, but it starts at £40, so 4 hours cost £160, not double the £100 for 2 hours. A 5 Ω heater's power, by P = I²R, starts at (0, 0) but curves upwards, from 20 W at 2 A to 80 W at 4 A, four times as much. OpenStax notes that if a V-I line is not straight, the material is not ohmic, so Ohm's law cannot be used for it.[^2] Read where the axes start, too, since a line running into a corner marked 20 cm misses (0, 0). With voltage up the side, RMIT calls R the slope of the V-I graph,[^3] so a [[steeper]] line means more ohms, and a 10 Ω line climbs twice as steeply as a 5 Ω one. Bitesize draws voltage on the y-axis and current on the x-axis,[^4] as this lesson does, but books differ and some put current up the side. Then the 5 Ω line is the steeper one, so read the axis labels first.

**Two amounts are in proportion when their graph is a straight line through (0, 0), like a resistor's V-I graph from V = IR. A line that misses (0, 0), or bends, is not in proportion. With voltage up the side, a steeper V-I line means more ohms, but read the axis labels first, as some books swap them.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** To test a graph for proportion, check that the line is straight and that it passes through (0, 0), reading where each axis starts. If both hold, doubling one amount doubles the other. On a V-I graph, read the axis labels before you judge steepness.

**Worked example:** A resistor reads 6 V at 2 A, and its V-I graph is a straight line through (0, 0). At 4 A, double the current, it reads 2 × 6 = 12 V. By V = IR it is a 3 Ω resistor, and 4 × 3 = 12 V checks it.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking any straight line as proportional. A cable drum weighing 20 kg empty plus 0.5 kg a metre makes a straight line, but it misses (0, 0), so 40 m of cable weighs 40 kg, not twice the 30 kg of 20 m.
- Taking a line from (0, 0) that bends as proportional. A part whose V-I line is not straight is not ohmic,[^2] so read its voltage off the curve rather than doubling.
- Taking the corner as (0, 0). If the side starts at 20 cm, a line from the corner starts at 20 cm, not 0.
- Judging steepness without the labels. With voltage up the side a steeper line means more ohms,[^3] but with current up the side the steeper line has fewer.
- Joining measured readings dot to dot. Lay one best-fit line through them, as in From a table to a graph, and see whether it runs through (0, 0).
